me-01.title: What Is a Machine?
explain: A **machine** is a device that transmits or converts force to help people do what they intend. The simplest machines are the **simple machines**, such as the lever, the pulley, and the inclined plane. A simple machine does not create force out of nothing. In exchange for changing the size or direction of a force, it gives up something else.

Here, **work** is the product of a force and the distance moved in the direction of that force. It is written $W = F \times d$. In an ideal machine with no friction, the work put in equals the work got out. Therefore, reducing the force means moving through a **greater distance** in the same proportion.

A **lever** is a machine that uses a bar rotating around a **fulcrum** (pivot point). The distance from the fulcrum to the point where force is applied is the effort arm, and the distance from the fulcrum to the load is the load arm. In an ideal lever, $F_{힘} \times (\text{힘팔}) = F_{짐} \times (\text{짐팔})$ holds. If the effort arm is three times as long as the load arm, the same load is lifted with one-third of the force.

explain.alt: A horizontal bar has a downward arrow at its left end labeled 'force ?'. The fulcrum is near the right side of the bar. The distance from the fulcrum to the left end is marked 1.5 m, and the distance to the right end is marked 0.5 m. A load labeled '60 N' sits on the right end.

explain: An **inclined plane** lets you push a load up at a slant instead of lifting it straight up. Ideally, $F = W \times \dfrac{h}{L}$. Here $W$ is the weight of the load, $h$ is the height it is raised, and $L$ is the length measured along the inclined plane.

explain.alt: A box rests on a right-triangle-shaped inclined plane and is labeled 'box 100 N'. The sloped side of the incline is marked 5 m, and the vertical height is marked 2 m.

explain: A **pulley** is a wheel over which a rope runs. A **fixed pulley**, attached to the ceiling, only changes the direction of the pull; the size of the force stays the same. A **movable pulley** moves together with the load. Because two strands of rope share the load, the force is ideally halved, but the rope must be pulled through twice the distance.

examples.title: Lifting a Stone with a Lever
body: Suppose a stone weighing 60 N is placed 0.5 m from the fulcrum, and you press down at a point 1.5 m from the fulcrum.

Since $F \times 1.5 = 60 \times 0.5$, we get $F = 20$ N. This is one-third of the force needed to lift the stone directly. In exchange, the end you press moves down three times as far as the stone rises.

me-02.title: Equilibrium of Forces
explain: **Force** is a quantity with both magnitude and direction, and its unit is the N (newton). A force can push or pull an object, and it can also make it **turn**. A door opens easily when pushed at the handle but hardly moves when pushed near the hinge; this is an example of turning.

The degree to which a force turns an object is called the **moment** (torque). If $d$ is the perpendicular distance from the center of rotation to the line of action of the force, then $M = F \times d$. The unit is N·m. For the same force, the larger $d$ is, the larger the moment. This is why a long wrench loosens a bolt easily.

An object that is at rest, neither moving nor rotating, is said to be in **equilibrium**. For an object in a plane, equilibrium requires both of the following conditions to hold.
- The sum of the forces is zero. The sum of the forces pushing upward equals the sum of the forces pushing downward.
- The sum of the moments about any chosen point is zero. The sum of the clockwise moments equals the sum of the counterclockwise moments.

To make the calculation easier, take as the reference point **the place where the unknown force acts**. The moment of that force is then zero, so it drops out of the equation.

Since the sum of the forces must be zero, the left person supports $100 - 25 = 75$ N. The person closer to the load supports more.

me-03.title: Deformation of Materials
explain: When a force acts on a material, the material stretches or shrinks. Even for the same force, a thin rod is more dangerous than a thick one. For this reason, we use not the force itself but the force per unit area.

**Stress** is the force divided by the cross-sectional area that carries it. $\sigma = \dfrac{F}{A}$. Its unit is N/m², which is called Pa (pascal). In engineering, N/mm² is often used, and $1\ \text{N/mm}^2 = 1\ \text{MPa}$.
**Strain** is the increase in length divided by the original length. $\varepsilon = \dfrac{\Delta L}{L_0}$. Since it is a length divided by a length, it has no unit.
If a rod is pulled slowly and stress and strain are plotted, a curve like the one below is obtained. The figure is simplified to show the concept. The actual curve differs from material to material.

explain.alt: A graph with strain on the horizontal axis and stress on the vertical axis. From the origin a straight line rises to point '가', then bends gently upward to the highest point '나', and then descends to end at point '다'. The section from the origin to '가' is labeled '구간 1', and the section from '가' to '다' is labeled '구간 2'.

explain: The first part of the curve (section 1) is nearly a straight line. In this section, when the force is removed, the material **returns to its original shape.** This is called **elastic deformation**. The steeper the slope of this section, the stiffer the material, meaning it stretches less under the same force.

In the later part (section 2), some of the deformation **remains permanently** even after the force is removed. This is called **plastic deformation**. It is like a paper clip: if it is bent slightly, it springs back, but if it is bent a lot, it stays bent. The highest point of the curve is the maximum stress the material can withstand, and at the end point the material breaks.

Pulling a rod with a cross-sectional area of 50 mm² with the same force gives 40 MPa, twice as much. If the material is the same, the thinner one reaches its limit first.

me-04.title: Heat and Engines
explain: A **heat engine** is a machine that converts part of the heat obtained by burning fuel into work. The gasoline engine of a car is a typical example. If $Q_{입력}$ is the heat obtained from the fuel and $W$ is the amount actually converted into work, the **thermal efficiency** is $\eta = \dfrac{W}{Q_{입력}}$.

The efficiency of a heat engine can never be 1. Heat that is not converted into work is discarded to the environment through hot exhaust gas and cooling water. For this reason, in many automobile engines more than half of the fuel energy is not converted into work.

A gasoline engine in a car is usually of the **four-stroke** type. A **stroke** is one upward or downward movement of the piston inside the cylinder. A four-stroke cycle repeats four strokes, and during one cycle the crankshaft turns two revolutions.
1. **Intake**: The intake passage opens and the piston moves down, drawing in a mixture of fuel and air.
2. **Compression**: All passages close and the piston moves up, compressing the mixture.
3. **Combustion (power)**: A spark ignites the mixture, and the expanding gas pushes the piston down. This is the only stroke that produces work.
4. **Exhaust**: The exhaust passage opens and the piston moves up, pushing out the burned gas.

explain.alt: Four cylinder drawings labeled '가', '나', '다', '라'. Above each cylinder are intake and exhaust passages; open passages are shown with green arrows and closed passages with ×. '가' has both passages closed, an orange spark, and the piston moving down. '나' has the intake passage open and the piston moving down. '다' has the exhaust passage open and the piston moving up. '라' has both passages closed and the piston moving up.

explain: The four cylinders in the figure are arranged in a sequence different from the order above. By the opening and closing of the passages, the direction of the piston, and the presence of a spark, you can tell which stroke each one shows.
A diesel engine also has four strokes, but it differs in that it compresses only air strongly and injects fuel into the heated air, where it ignites.

me-05.title: Gears and Power Transmission
explain: Transmitting the rotation produced by an engine or motor to where it is needed, while appropriately changing its speed and force, is called **power transmission**. The representative component is the **gear** (toothed wheel). Meshed gears turn by pushing one tooth at a time.

explain.alt: Two meshed toothed wheels. The smaller wheel on the left is labeled 'driving (input)', with '20 teeth' inside it and a clockwise direction. The larger wheel on the right is labeled 'driven (output)', with '40 teeth' inside it and a counterclockwise direction.

explain: The gear that applies the force is called the **driving gear**, and the gear that receives it is the **driven gear**. Letting the numbers of teeth be $z_1$ and $z_2$ respectively, in this lesson the **gear ratio** is defined as $i = \dfrac{z_2}{z_1}$. In the figure, $40 / 20 = 2$.

In two meshed gears, the same number of teeth passes the contact point at a time. Therefore the rotational speed (rpm) is inversely proportional to the number of teeth: $n_2 = n_1 \times \dfrac{z_1}{z_2}$. A larger driven gear turns more slowly.

The force, on the other hand, increases. If there is no friction loss, the torque is $T_2 = T_1 \times \dfrac{z_2}{z_1}$. Power is $P = T \times \omega$, which ideally stays the same during transmission. If the speed is halved, the torque doubles. This is the exchange of distance and force seen in lesson 1, now appearing in rotation.
Meshed gears rotate in **opposite directions**. If they must turn in the same direction, another gear is inserted between them, or they are connected by a chain or belt.

body: A driving gear with 20 teeth turns at 120 revolutions per minute (120 rpm), and the driven gear has 40 teeth. Then $n_2 = 120 \times 20 / 40 = 60$ rpm.
With the same gears, the torque doubles. Speed is given up in exchange for gaining force.

me-06.title: The Design Process
explain: A mechanical engineer does not only select finished parts. Starting from a need, the engineer carries out **design**, which means creating a solution. Design is not finished in one pass; it is a process of going back and revising.

explain.alt: Four boxes connected by arrows, in order: '1 Problem definition', '2 Ideas', '3 Prototype', '4 Testing'. An orange arrow goes from the fourth box back to the second box and is labeled 'If the requirements are not met, go back'.

explain:
1. **Problem definition**: Decide what to solve, and write down measurable **requirements** and the **constraints** that must be kept (size, budget, materials, etc.).
2. **Ideas**: Propose several solutions and compare them against the requirements to choose one. At this stage, the lever, gear, and stress calculations learned earlier are used.
3. **Prototype**: Build a model or a first product that can be tested.
4. **Testing**: Check the requirements numerically. If they are not met, return to the idea stage and revise.
A good requirement must be **measurable**. "Sturdy and convenient" cannot be tested, but "can be pushed with one hand using a force of 20 N or less" can be confirmed with a force sensor.

This lesson is only an introduction to a way of thinking about design. The safety and standards of an actual product cannot be judged with calculations at this level; they are handled by professional engineers and the relevant standards.

examples.title: Hypothetical Case: A Book Cart for a Village Library
body: At a hypothetical village library, a book cart keeps catching on the threshold at the entrance. The librarian must be able to push it with one hand.
Problem definition: The loaded book cart must be pushable over the threshold with one hand using a force of 20 N or less. Constraints: width of 60 cm or less, and a budget limit.

Ideas: enlarge the wheels / place a small inclined plane at the threshold / lengthen the handle. Since an inclined plane reduces the force needed, as learned in lesson 1, it is chosen for a prototype.
Testing: push the cart five times, measure the force, and compare it with the requirement. If the requirement is not met, make the inclined plane longer and test again.

me-07.title: Axial Stress and Thermal Stress
explain: In the first stage we looked at the basics of stress and strain and the stress–strain curve. Now we apply them to actual members. The cables of a bridge, the columns of a building, and the bolts of an engine all carry axial forces. How much do they stretch, and how much force can they withstand? And what about the case where no force is applied, but a change in temperature alone creates stress?

For a member under an axial load $P$ with cross-sectional area $A$, the **normal stress** is $\sigma = P/A$, and the **strain** is $\varepsilon = \delta/L$ ($\delta$ is the change in length). Within the elastic range, **Hooke's law** $\sigma = E\varepsilon$ ($E$ is the modulus of elasticity) holds, so the elongation is $$\delta = \frac{PL}{AE}$$ 이다. 같은 힘이라도 길고 가늘고 부드러운(작은 $E$) 부재일수록 많이 늘어난다. 강철은 $E \approx 200$ GPa, 알루미늄은 약 70 GPa이다. (In English: this is the elongation. Under the same force, a member that is longer, thinner, and softer (smaller E) stretches more. Steel has E of about 200 GPa, and aluminum about 70 GPa.)

When a material is stretched, it becomes thinner sideways. The ratio of the lateral strain to the longitudinal strain is called **Poisson's ratio** $\nu$, and for metals it is about 0.3. Where the cross-section changes abruptly (holes, grooves, corners), **stress concentration** occurs, in which the stress becomes several times the average. Failure usually starts at such places, so corners are rounded.

**Thermal stress**: Materials expand as the temperature rises. If a member can expand freely, it elongates by $\delta_T = \alpha\Delta T L$ ($\alpha$ is the coefficient of thermal expansion), and no stress arises. However, if both ends are fixed so that it cannot elongate, it is as if the fixed supports compress it back by that amount, and a stress of $$\sigma_T = E\alpha\Delta T$$ arises. It is surprising that this does not depend on the length. This is why railway rails have gaps between joints, and why long pipes have bent expansion joints.

Limitations: These formulas hold under the assumptions that the load acts through the center of the cross-section, the material is homogeneous, and the behavior stays within the elastic range. When a slender member is under **compression**, it may bend sideways, a phenomenon called **buckling**, before the material reaches its strength (column buckling in civil engineering). This lesson covers concepts and calculations; it is not a guideline for judging the safety of actual structures.

examples.title: Elongation of a Steel Rod
body: Conditions: length 2 m, cross-sectional area 100 mm² $= 10^{-4}$ m², tensile load 20 kN, $E = 200$ GPa.
Step 1: stress $\sigma = 20000/10^{-4} = 200$ MPa.
Step 2: $\delta = PL/(AE) = 20000 \times 2/(10^{-4} \times 2 \times 10^{11}) = 0.002$ m $= 2$ mm. Strain is 0.1%.

Step 1: $\sigma_T = 200 \times 10^9 \times 12 \times 10^{-6} \times 30 = 72$ MPa (compression).
Step 2: The stress is 72 MPa regardless of the rail length. A large compressive stress creates a risk of buckling, in which the rail bends sideways.

me-08.title: Shear Force and Bending Moment Diagrams
explain: A long member that bears loads perpendicular to its axis, such as a bridge deck, a shelf, or the arm of a crane, is called a **beam**. To design a beam, you must first know at which position along it the internal forces are greatest. The map for this is the **shear force diagram** (SFD) and the **bending moment diagram** (BMD).

If a beam is imaginarily cut at some position, the cut surface has two kinds of internal force: the **shear force** $V$, which tends to slide the two faces up and down relative to each other, and the **bending moment** $M$, which tends to bend the beam. Both are found from the **equilibrium of forces** (step 1) applied to one of the cut-off parts. Establish a sign convention and use it consistently.

explain.alt: Diagram of a simply supported beam. A beam 4 m long has its left end A supported by a pin and its right end B supported by a roller, with a 10 kN downward load P at the center. The shear force diagram below is a step shape: +5 kN over the left half and −5 kN over the right half. Below it, the bending moment diagram is a triangle that is zero at both ends and largest at the center, labeled 'maximum M = ?'.

explain: Consider the simply supported beam in the figure (length $L$, concentrated load $P$ at the center). ① By symmetry, each support reaction is $P/2$. ② Cutting at a distance $x$ from the left end (to the left of the load), the shear force is $V = P/2$ and the bending moment is $M = \frac{P}{2}x$. ③ Passing the load, the shear force drops abruptly by $P$ and becomes $-P/2$. ④ The moment is largest at the center, $M_{max} = \frac{PL}{4}$, and is zero at both ends.

The relationships between the diagrams make them easier to draw. **The shear force is the slope of the bending moment**: $\frac{dM}{dx} = V$. In a region where the shear force is positive, the moment increases, and the moment is largest where the shear force becomes zero (changes sign). Also, if there is a distributed load $w$, then $\frac{dV}{dx} = -w$, so the shear force changes linearly and the moment changes parabolically. The maximum moment of a simple beam under a uniformly distributed load is $\frac{wL^2}{8}$.

Limitations: This analysis assumes that the beam bends only slightly (small deformation) and that the support conditions are ideal (perfect pins and rollers). A **statically indeterminate beam** (such as one with both ends fixed), in which there are more unknown reactions than equilibrium equations, requires additional deformation conditions to solve. This lesson covers concepts and calculations; it is not a guideline for actual structural design.

Step 1: each reaction is 5 kN. The distance to the center is 2 m.
Step 2: $M_{max} = 5 \times 2 = 10$ kN·m $= PL/4$. It is largest at the center, where the shear force changes sign from +5 to −5.

me-09.title: Bending Stress, Section Design, and Safety Factor
explain: In the previous lesson we learned where a large bending moment acts on a beam. Now we cover what stress that moment creates within the cross-section of the beam, and what shape the cross-section should have to be efficient. Why are steel columns and beams mostly I-shaped?

When a beam bends downward, its top surface is compressed and its bottom surface is stretched. Somewhere in between is the **neutral axis**, where the length does not change. The bending stress is zero at the neutral axis and increases linearly with distance from it. $$\sigma = \frac{My}{I}$$ $y$는 중립축으로부터의 거리, $I$는 **단면 2차 모멘트**다. 최대 응력은 가장 바깥 면($y = c$)에서 $\sigma_{max} = Mc/I = M/S$이고, $S = I/c$를 **단면계수**라 한다. (In English: here y is the distance from the neutral axis and I is the second moment of area. The maximum stress occurs at the outermost surface (y = c), where sigma_max = Mc/I = M/S, and S = I/c is called the section modulus.)

The **second moment of area** measures how far the area of a cross-section is distributed from the neutral axis. For a rectangle of width $b$ and height $h$, $I = \frac{bh^3}{12}$. The height enters as a cube. This is why the same ruler bends easily when laid flat, but resists bending when stood on its edge. An **I-shaped section** concentrates material in the upper and lower parts (flanges) far from the neutral axis, making $I$ large with the same amount of material. It removes material near the neutral axis, where there is almost no stress.

The **safety factor** is the ratio of the strength the material can withstand to the actual stress: $n = \frac{\sigma_{\text{허용 기준}}}{\sigma_{실제}}$. For ductile materials, the yield strength is used as the criterion. If the safety factor is 2, the actual stress is half the yield strength. The safety factor is chosen according to the uncertainty in estimating loads, variation in materials, deterioration such as corrosion and fatigue, and how serious the consequences of failure would be. Structures where people may be injured use a larger safety factor.

Limitations: $\sigma = My/I$ is a result of the assumptions that the cross-section stays plane after bending and that behavior remains within the elastic range. Members under repeated loads can fail by **fatigue**, in which cracks grow and cause failure at stresses far below the yield strength (Materials Science and Engineering, stage 4). The safety factor is a "margin" that covers these uncertainties, not an exact prediction of failure. This lesson covers concepts and is not a guideline for judging actual structural design.

examples.title: Maximum Stress in a Rectangular Beam
body: Conditions: a wooden beam 0.05 m wide and 0.1 m high, with a maximum bending moment of 1 kN·m.
Step 1: $I = 0.05 \times 0.1^3/12 \approx 4.17 \times 10^{-6}$ m⁴, $c = 0.05$ m, $S = I/c \approx 8.33 \times 10^{-5}$ m³.
Step 2: $\sigma_{max} = 1000/8.33 \times 10^{-5} = 12$ MPa. If the same beam is laid flat (width 0.1, height 0.05), $S$ is halved and the stress doubles to 24 MPa.

examples.title: Judging the Safety Factor
body: Conditions: steel with a yield strength of 250 MPa, and a calculated maximum bending stress of 100 MPa.

Analysis: the safety factor is 2.5. If the required safety factor is 3, the cross-section must be enlarged to bring the stress down to about 83 MPa or less. Increasing the height slightly is more effective than increasing the width ($I \propto h^3$).

me-10.title: Heat Engine Cycles: Otto and Rankine
explain: In the first stage we briefly looked at the principle by which an engine converts heat into work. In Physics stage 3 we learned that Carnot efficiency is the theoretical upper limit. Actual engines and power plants operate on practical cycles other than the Carnot cycle. This lesson covers the **Otto cycle**, an idealized model of the gasoline engine in a car, and the **Rankine cycle** of the steam power plant.

**Otto cycle** (idealized): ① adiabatic compression (the piston compresses the air-fuel mixture) → ② constant-volume heating (instantaneous combustion at ignition) → ③ adiabatic expansion (power stroke) → ④ constant-volume heat rejection (exhaust). The thermal efficiency depends only on the **compression ratio** $r = V_{max}/V_{min}$. $$\eta_{Otto} = 1 - \frac{1}{r^{\gamma - 1}}$$ 공기에서 $\gamma \approx 1.4$이다. 압축비 8이면 $1 - 8^{-0.4} \approx 56\%$, 압축비 10이면 약 60%다. (In English: for air, gamma is about 1.4. A compression ratio of 8 gives 1 - 8^(-0.4), about 56%, and a ratio of 10 gives about 60%.)

Raising the compression ratio continually increases efficiency, but a gasoline engine is limited in compression ratio by **knocking**, in which the mixture ignites on its own before the spark during compression. A diesel engine compresses only air to create a high temperature and then injects fuel. It can therefore use a higher compression ratio (15–20) without concern about knocking, and its efficiency is higher.

The **Rankine cycle** uses water as the working fluid. ① Raise the pressure of the water with a pump (little work is required, since liquids are easy to compress) → ② heat it in a boiler to make high-pressure steam → ③ expand the steam in a turbine to do work → ④ cool it in a condenser to turn it back into water. The pump work is very small compared with the turbine work, so the net work is large. Efficiency $= \frac{W_{터빈} - W_{펌프}}{Q_{보일러}}$. This is the basic cycle of actual thermal and nuclear power plants.

Ways to raise efficiency: raise the boiler temperature and pressure (a high-temperature source), and lower the condensing temperature (a low-temperature sink). This is in the same direction as the Carnot efficiency $1 - T_C/T_H$. Actual efficiency is lower than that of the ideal cycle because of friction, heat losses, and irreversible processes. Limitation: the ideal cycles are simplifications that assume the working fluid is an ideal gas (Otto) or in equilibrium states (Rankine); actual design uses measured property tables and loss models.

examples.title: Compression Ratio and Otto Efficiency
body: Conditions: $\gamma = 1.4$, compression ratios 8 and 12.
Step 1: $8^{0.4} \approx 2.297$, efficiency $\approx 1 - 0.435 = 56.5\%$.

Step 2: $12^{0.4} \approx 2.702$, efficiency $\approx 63\%$. Raising the compression ratio by a factor of 1.5 raises the ideal efficiency by about 6.5 percentage points. Actual engine efficiency is well below this because of losses.

body: Conditions (idealized): heat supplied by the boiler 3000 kJ/kg, turbine work 1000 kJ/kg, pump work 10 kJ/kg.
Step 1: net work $= 1000 - 10 = 990$ kJ/kg.
Step 2: efficiency $= 990/3000 = 33\%$. The heat discarded in the condenser is $3000 - 990 = 2010$ kJ/kg, so two-thirds of the supplied heat leaves with the cooling water.

me-11.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection, Radiation, and Thermal Resistance
explain: How quickly a house cools in winter, how a computer chip is cooled, and how many minutes it takes for coffee to become drinkable are all problems of **heat transfer**. Thermodynamics tells us how much heat is transferred, while heat transfer tells us how **quickly** it is transferred. There are three modes.

**Conduction**: Heat flows as molecular motion is passed to neighboring molecules within a body. According to Fourier's law, the heat flow through a plate of thickness $L$ and area $A$ is $\dot{Q} = kA\frac{\Delta T}{L}$. $k$ is the thermal conductivity; it is about 400 for copper, about 1 for concrete, and about 0.04 W/(m·K) for insulation. **Convection**: A fluid moves and carries heat with it. Newton's law of cooling is $\dot{Q} = hA(T_s - T_\infty)$, where $h$ is the convective heat transfer coefficient, which becomes larger as the wind gets stronger. **Radiation**: Heat is transferred by electromagnetic waves and requires no medium. $\dot{Q} = \varepsilon\sigma A(T_s^4 - T_{sur}^4)$.

The concept of **thermal resistance** simplifies calculations. In analogy with Ohm's law ($I = V/R$) for electric circuits, writing $\dot{Q} = \Delta T/R_{th}$, the conduction resistance is $R = \frac{L}{kA}$ and the convection resistance is $R = \frac{1}{hA}$. A wall made of several layers has its resistances added **in series**. You can use the intuition of electric circuit analysis directly (Electrical and Electronic Engineering, stage 2).

explain.alt: A wall with two layers. On the indoor side at 20°C is a brick layer (thickness 0.2 m, thermal conductivity k = 0.8 W/(m·K)). Outside it is an insulation layer (thickness 0.05 m, k = 0.04), and the outdoor temperature is −10°C. It deals with the heat flow through 1 m² of wall and notes that the surface convective resistance is ignored.

explain: For the wall in the figure, the resistance per unit area (1 m²) is $0.2/0.8 = 0.25$ for the brick and $0.05/0.04 = 1.25$ m²·K/W for the insulation, totaling 1.5. The thin insulation has five times the resistance of the thick brick. The heat flow is $30/1.5 = 20$ W/m². Without the insulation it would be $30/0.25 = 120$ W/m², six times as much. Limitations: real walls have surface convective resistance, heat leaking through windows and joints (thermal bridging), and the effects of moisture. This lesson covers concepts and calculations; it is not a guideline for judging the energy performance of buildings.

body: Conditions: the wall in the figure, with a heat flow of 20 W/m².
Step 1: the temperature drop across the brick layer $= 20 \times 0.25 = 5$ K. The temperature at the brick–insulation boundary $= 20 - 5 = 15$°C.

Step 2: the temperature drop across the insulation layer $= 20 \times 1.25 = 25$ K, so the outer surface is at $15 - 25 = -10$°C. The temperature drop is divided in proportion to the resistances (the same as voltage division).

me-12.title: Refrigeration Cycles and the Coefficient of Performance
explain: Refrigerators and air conditioners move heat **from a cold place to a hot place**. According to the Clausius statement learned in Physics stage 3, this does not happen spontaneously. In exchange, **work** must be supplied. This lesson covers the **refrigeration cycle**, which runs a heat engine in reverse, and how its performance is measured.

**Vapor-compression refrigeration cycle**: ① The compressor compresses low-pressure refrigerant vapor to high pressure and high temperature (work input). ② In the condenser, the refrigerant releases heat to the outside (the hot side) and becomes liquid. ③ As it passes through the expansion valve, the pressure drops sharply and the refrigerant becomes cold. ④ In the evaporator, the refrigerant absorbs heat from the inside (the cold side) and evaporates. The refrigerant takes advantage of the property that it boils at a low temperature when the pressure is low.

The performance of a refrigerator is measured not by efficiency but by the **coefficient of performance** (COP). For a refrigerator (cooling), $COP_R = \frac{Q_L}{W}$ (heat removed from the cold side ÷ work input). For a heat pump (heating), $COP_{HP} = \frac{Q_H}{W}$ (heat delivered to the hot side ÷ work). From energy conservation, $Q_H = Q_L + W$, so $COP_{HP} = COP_R + 1$. The COP can be greater than 1 and is usually 3 to 5. Putting in work 1 moves heat of 3 to 5. This is because the device does not create energy but **moves** it.

The theoretical upper limit is the Carnot refrigerator: $COP_{R,max} = \frac{T_L}{T_H - T_L}$ (kelvin). The smaller the temperature difference between the two sides, the larger the COP. So the closer an air conditioner's set temperature is to the outdoor temperature, the less electricity is needed for cooling. A heat pump for heating can supply several times as much heat as an electric heater (COP = 1, which converts electricity directly into heat) with the same electricity, but when the outdoors is very cold, the temperature difference grows and the COP drops.

Limitations and environment: The actual COP is much lower than the Carnot limit because of compressor losses and the temperature differences across heat exchangers. The choice of refrigerant must consider environmental impact as well as performance. Some refrigerants used in the past deplete the ozone layer or are powerful greenhouse gases, so they are being phased down under international agreements. This lesson covers principles and is not a guide to refrigerant handling or equipment work methods.

me-13.title: Hydrostatic Pressure and Buoyancy
explain: Divers' ears hurt the deeper they go, and the wall of a dam is thicker at the bottom than at the top. A steel ship weighing tens of thousands of tons floats on water. All of these are explained by the pressure of a **fluid at rest**, called hydrostatic pressure. It is the starting point of fluid mechanics.

In a fluid at rest, the pressure increases by the weight of the column of fluid above as you go down a depth $h$. $$p = p_0 + \rho g h$$ This is the same principle as static equilibrium in Earth Science stage 3 (for liquids, the density is nearly constant, so it is simpler). In water, the pressure increases by about 1 atm (about 100 kPa) for every 10 m of descent. The pressure depends only on depth and is **independent of the shape of the container**.

**Pascal's principle**: A pressure applied at one point of an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions. In a hydraulic jack, a small piston (area $A_1$) receives a force $F_1$, and the large piston (area $A_2$) produces a force $F_2 = F_1\frac{A_2}{A_1}$. The force is larger, but the large piston moves a shorter distance by the same ratio, so work is conserved (as with a lever).

The **total force** acting on the wall of a dam or floodgate is the sum, over the area, of the pressure that grows with depth. For a vertical wall of width $b$ and depth $H$ (excluding atmospheric pressure), the total force is the average pressure $\rho g H/2$ multiplied by the area $bH$, that is, $F = \frac{1}{2}\rho g b H^2$. If the depth doubles, the force becomes four times as large. Since the force is greater at the lower part, the point of action is at a height of $H/3$ above the bottom.

**Archimedes' principle**: An object submerged in a fluid experiences an upward force (buoyancy) equal to the **weight of the fluid it displaces**. $F_B = \rho_{유체}gV_{잠긴}$. If the object's density is less than that of the fluid, it floats partly submerged, and the fraction of its volume that is submerged equals the ratio of the densities. A steel ship floats because it is hollow, so the average density of the whole ship (steel plus air) is less than that of water. Limitation: the stability of a ship depends not only on buoyancy but also on the positions of its center of gravity and center of buoyancy. This lesson covers principles and calculations; it is not a design guideline for ships or dams.

me-14.title: The Continuity Equation and Bernoulli's Equation
explain: If you cover the end of a hose with your finger, the water shoots out faster and farther. The air around an airplane wing moves at different speeds above and below the wing, which creates a pressure difference. Two basic equations for moving fluids explain these phenomena. One expresses **conservation of mass** and the other expresses **conservation of energy**.

**Continuity equation**: For an incompressible fluid flowing in a pipe, the volume passing per unit time (the **flow rate**) is the same everywhere along the pipe. $$Q = A_1v_1 = A_2v_2$$ Where the pipe narrows, the velocity increases. If the cross-sectional area is halved, the velocity doubles. This is because whatever flows in must flow out (conservation of mass).

explain.alt: A horizontal pipe narrows in the middle and then widens again. The cross-sectional area of the wide part is 0.02 m², with velocity v₁ = 2 m/s. The cross-sectional area of the narrow part is 0.01 m², and its velocity v₂ is shown as a question mark. Water (density 1000 kg/m³) flows through it.

explain: **Bernoulli's equation**: For a steady, inviscid flow of an incompressible fluid, along the same streamline, $$p + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g z = \text{일정}$$ holds. This means that the sum of pressure energy, kinetic energy, and potential energy (per unit volume) is conserved. At the same height, **the pressure is lower where the speed is higher**. As in the figure, where the pipe narrows and the speed increases, the pressure drops. The **Venturi flow meter** is a device that finds the flow speed by measuring this pressure difference.

Applications: The speed of water exiting a hole in the bottom of a tank is $v = \sqrt{2gh}$ (Torricelli's theorem), the same as the speed of an object falling from the same height. A **Pitot tube** measures an airplane's speed from the difference between the pressure at a point where the flow is blocked head-on and the pressure on the side. Limitation: the key assumption of Bernoulli's equation is that there is **no friction (viscosity)**. In real pipe flows, energy is lost to friction, so the pressure drops further downstream. This loss is treated in the next lesson. Also, the common explanation that "the air above the wing must travel a longer path in the same time, so it is faster" is incorrect; lift must be understood together with the effect of the wing turning the airflow downward.

me-15.title: Reynolds Number and Pipe Friction Losses
explain: When a faucet is opened slightly, the stream of water is smooth and clear, but when it is opened wide, it becomes disordered and foamy. Fluid flow has two appearances: orderly **laminar flow** and irregular **turbulent flow**. Depending on which one occurs, the energy lost in the pipe, that is, the work the pump must do, differs greatly.

The dimensionless number that determines the appearance of the flow is the **Reynolds number**. $$Re = \frac{\rho v D}{\mu}$$ ($D$ 관 지름, $\mu$ 점성계수). 관성력(흐름을 흐트러뜨리려는 경향)과 점성력(흐름을 질서 있게 붙잡는 경향)의 비다. 원형관에서 대략 $Re < 2300$이면 층류, $Re > 4000$이면 난류, 그 사이는 전이 영역이다. 물은 점성이 작아 일상적인 배관 흐름은 대부분 난류다. (In English: D is the pipe diameter and mu is the viscosity. Re is the ratio of inertial force, the tendency to disturb the flow, to viscous force, the tendency to hold the flow in order. In a circular pipe, roughly Re < 2300 gives laminar flow, Re > 4000 gives turbulent flow, and the range between is a transition region. Because water has low viscosity, most everyday piping flows are turbulent.)

The pressure (head) loss due to pipe friction is calculated with the **Darcy–Weisbach equation**. $$\Delta p = f\frac{L}{D}\frac{\rho v^2}{2}$$ $f$는 마찰계수다. 층류에서는 $f = 64/Re$로 이론적으로 정해지고, 난류에서는 레이놀즈수와 관 내벽의 **거칠기**에 따라 실험으로 정한다(무디 선도). 손실은 관 길이에 비례하고, 지름에 반비례하며, **유속의 제곱**에 비례한다. (In English: f is the friction factor. In laminar flow it is fixed theoretically as f = 64/Re; in turbulent flow it is determined experimentally, depending on the Reynolds number and the roughness of the inner pipe wall (the Moody chart). The loss is proportional to the pipe length, inversely proportional to the diameter, and proportional to the square of the velocity.)

Implications for design: when the same flow rate is sent, reducing the pipe diameter increases the velocity ($v \propto 1/D^2$), and the loss rises sharply, roughly as $v^2/D \propto 1/D^5$. Slightly increasing the pipe diameter can greatly reduce pump power, but the piping cost increases. This trade-off is the core of piping design. **Minor losses** arising from valves, bends, and sudden expansions or contractions are added separately.

Limitations: The boundary values of the Reynolds number (2300 and 4000) are rough criteria and depend on inlet conditions and vibration. Turbulence is still one of the unsolved problems of physics, so practice relies on empirical formulas and experimental data. This lesson covers concepts and calculations; it is not a guideline for actual piping design.

me-16.title: Natural Frequency and Avoiding Resonance
explain: When a washing machine starts its spin cycle, it shakes violently at a certain speed, then grows calm as it speeds up further. Every mechanical structure has **natural frequencies** at which it tends to vibrate by itself. When an external periodic force matches one of these frequencies, **resonance** occurs and the amplitude grows large. Resonance leads to noise, fatigue failure, and, in severe cases, structural collapse.

For a single-degree-of-freedom system modeled as a mass $m$ and a spring of stiffness $k$, the **natural angular frequency** is $\omega_n = \sqrt{k/m}$, as seen in Physics stage 2, and the natural frequency is $f_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$. The higher the stiffness and the smaller the mass, the higher the frequency. Actual structures have several natural frequencies (vibration modes), and the lowest one is usually the most important.

explain.alt: Horizontal axis: frequency ratio r = ω/ωₙ from 0 to 3. Vertical axis: amplitude magnification from 0 to 6. There are three curves for damping ratios ζ = 0.1, 0.3, and 0.7. All of them start at 1 when r = 0. The ζ = 0.1 curve rises sharply to about 5 near r = 1, the ζ = 0.3 curve rises gently to about 1.7, and the ζ = 0.7 curve barely rises. When r exceeds about 1.4, all the curves fall below 1 and keep decreasing.

explain: When an external force $F_0\cos\omega t$ acts, the steady-state amplitude is the static displacement $F_0/k$ multiplied by the **amplitude magnification factor**. $$\frac{X}{F_0/k} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(1 - r^2)^2 + (2\zeta r)^2}}, \quad r = \frac{\omega}{\omega_n}$$ $\zeta$는 **감쇠비**다. 그림처럼 $r = 1$ 근처에서 배율이 솟는다. $r = 1$에서 배율은 $\frac{1}{2\zeta}$로, 감쇠가 작을수록 매우 커진다($\zeta = 0.1$이면 5배). (In English: zeta is the damping ratio. As in the figure, the magnification rises sharply near r = 1. At r = 1 the magnification is 1/(2 zeta), which becomes very large as the damping decreases: 5 times for zeta = 0.1.)

Basic principles for **avoiding resonance**: design so that the operating frequency is far from the natural frequency. It is common to keep the operating range outside about ±20–30% of the natural frequency. The methods are ① changing the stiffness (adding reinforcement), ② changing the mass to shift the natural frequency, and ③ increasing the damping to lower the resonance peak. Rotating machines are designed to pass **quickly through** the natural frequency while speeding up to operating speed.

Limitations: The single-degree-of-freedom model is a simplification. Real structures have several modes and nonlinearity (stiffness changes at large amplitudes), and large vibrations can also arise from mechanisms other than periodic external forces, such as vortex-induced vibration from wind. This lesson covers concepts and calculations; it is not a guideline for judging the vibration safety of actual structures.

me-17.title: Damping and Vibration Isolation
explain: The rubber feet under a washing machine, the shock absorbers of a car, and the vibration-isolation table of precision equipment all deal with vibration. Vibration problems come in two directions: keeping a machine's vibration from being **transmitted** to the floor and buildings, and keeping floor vibration from **entering** precision equipment. Both are called **vibration isolation**, and the key tools are springs and **damping**.

**Damping** reduces vibration by converting vibrational energy into heat. A system with viscous damping $c$ follows $m\ddot{x} + c\dot{x} + kx = 0$, and its behavior is divided by the damping ratio $\zeta = \frac{c}{2\sqrt{mk}}$ (a second-order differential equation from Mathematics stage 5). If $\zeta < 1$, the amplitude decreases while the system oscillates (underdamped). If $\zeta = 1$, it returns to equilibrium as quickly as possible without oscillating (critically damped). If $\zeta > 1$, it returns to equilibrium slowly without oscillating (overdamped). Automobile suspensions are often designed with a value of about 0.2 to 0.4 for ride comfort and road grip.

The **transmissibility** is the ratio of the force transmitted to the floor (or the displacement transmitted in) to the original magnitude. It is determined by the frequency ratio $r = \omega/\omega_n$, and the important conclusion is that **the transmissibility becomes less than 1 only when $r > \sqrt{2}$**. That is, to obtain an isolation effect, the natural frequency of the support must be **lower** than $1/\sqrt{2}$ times the excitation frequency. For this reason, vibration isolation supports are made **soft** (small $k$).

Here a paradox of damping arises. For $r < \sqrt{2}$ (especially near resonance), more damping reduces the transmissibility and is advantageous. But in the isolation region $r > \sqrt{2}$, more damping actually makes the transmissibility slightly **larger**, because the damper connects the floor and the machine and thus transmits force. Therefore isolation supports are made soft, but a moderate amount of damping is provided for passing through resonance during startup and shutdown.

Limitations: If the support is made too soft, the static deflection becomes large and the machine wobbles, becoming unstable (static deflection $\delta = mg/k$, $\omega_n = \sqrt{g/\delta}$). Also, when vibrations in several directions and rotational vibrations occur together, single-degree-of-freedom analysis is insufficient. This lesson covers concepts and is not a guideline for actual vibration isolation design.

me-18.title: Feedback Control of Mechanical Systems
explain: A robot arm stops exactly at a set position, the nozzle of a 3D printer keeps a constant temperature, and cruise control holds the same speed on a hill. All of these are made possible by **feedback control**, which looks at measured values and corrects its own operation. This lesson covers the structure of control and the operation of the PID controller from the viewpoint of mechanical systems.

Components of a control system: the **setpoint** (the desired position), the **sensor** (which measures the actual position), the **comparator** (error = setpoint − measurement), the **controller** (which computes the control action from the error), the **actuator** (a motor or heater), and the **plant** (the controlled object, such as the robot arm). **Open-loop control**, which has no feedback (for example, a timer that turns a heater on for a fixed time), is simple but cannot respond to disturbances such as an opened door. **Closed-loop control** sees the error and corrects it even when a disturbance occurs.

The output of a **PID controller** is $u(t) = K_Pe(t) + K_I\int e\,dt + K_D\frac{de}{dt}$. The proportional term responds immediately, in proportion to the error. Increasing the gain $K_P$ makes the response faster but increases overshoot and vibration. The integral term accumulates the error and eventually drives the steady-state error to zero, which is needed to overcome a disturbance that keeps acting, such as gravity. The derivative term applies braking in advance when the error is decreasing quickly, which reduces overshoot. It plays the same role as damping in the previous lesson.

**Tuning**: Usually $K_P$ is increased first to make the response quick, the remaining error is eliminated with $K_I$, and the oscillation is reduced with $K_D$. The measures for evaluating the response are rise time, overshoot (%), settling time, and steady-state error. For a second-order system, the overshoot is determined by the damping ratio. A damping ratio of about 0.7 gives an overshoot of about 5%, a balance point that is fast without overshooting much.

Limitations and practical problems: Actuators have limits, so when the motor voltage or heater output is at its maximum (saturation), the integral term keeps accumulating and causes a large overshoot, called **integral windup**. The derivative term amplifies sensor noise. **Time delay** in sensors and actuators can make the system unstable. Real controllers include devices that guard against these problems. This lesson covers concepts and is not a guideline for actual machine control settings.

me-19.title: Integrated Problem Solving: Review of a Cooling Water Pump System
explain: The first lesson of the capstone reviews one hypothetical mechanical system together, using knowledge from stages 2 to 5. System: to cool factory equipment, a pump sends water through pipes, through a heat exchanger, and back. The pump sits on a steel base.

**Stage 1 (flow rate and heat)**: Take 60 kW of heat from the equipment into the water, while keeping the rise in water temperature to 10 K or less. The required mass flow rate is $\dot{m} = \frac{\dot{Q}}{c\Delta T} = \frac{60000}{4186 \times 10} \approx 1.43$ kg/s, and the volumetric flow rate is about 0.00143 m³/s.

**Stage 2 (fluid)**: With a pipe of diameter 0.04 m (cross-sectional area about $1.26 \times 10^{-3}$ m²), the velocity is $v \approx 1.14$ m/s and the Reynolds number is $\approx 1000 \times 1.14 \times 0.04/0.001 \approx 45{,}600$, so the flow is turbulent. Estimating the friction factor as 0.022 and the pipe length as 50 m, $\Delta p = 0.022 \times (50/0.04) \times 1000 \times 1.14^2/2 \approx 17.9$ kPa. The pump must overcome the total pressure loss, obtained by adding the minor losses and the heat exchanger loss. Pump power (work delivered to the fluid) $= Q\Delta p_{total}$.

**Stage 3 (structure)**: For the base beam that supports the pump and motor weight of 80 kg (length 0.8 m, simply supported, load at the center), the maximum bending moment is $= 80 \times 9.8 \times 0.8/4 \approx 157$ N·m. Choose a cross-section so that the bending stress is at or below the allowable criterion.

**Stage 4 (vibration)**: The pump runs at 2,900 rpm (about 48 Hz). If the natural frequency of the base and pump is near 48 Hz, resonance occurs. Adding rubber mounts to lower the natural frequency to about 15 Hz places the system in the isolation region, $r \approx 3.2 > \sqrt{2}$. Checking with the static deflection, $\delta = g/\omega_n^2 \approx 9.8/(2\pi \times 15)^2 \approx 1.1$ mm.

**Stage 5 (control and critique)**: To keep the outlet temperature constant, a temperature sensor and a PI controller adjust the pump speed. **Critique**: Increasing the flow rate improves heat removal, but the pressure loss grows with the square of the velocity, so the pump power rises sharply. Changing the pump speed also changes the excitation frequency, so the system may pass through a resonance band. The decisions in each field are intertwined, so optimizing only one creates problems in the others.

Step 2: The pump power drops to about one third. In exchange, pipe material costs and installation space increase. The choice is made by comparing electricity costs over the operating period with the initial cost.

Analysis: $r = 20/15 \approx 1.33 < \sqrt{2}$, so the isolation effect disappears and the system approaches the resonance band. If low-speed operation is needed, the mounts must be made softer or the damping increased.

me-20.title: Bachelor's Capstone: Integrated Design Review Report for a Mechanical System
explain: The final task is to **choose one hypothetical mechanical system, write a design review report that examines at least three of the fields of strength, heat, fluid, vibration, and control together, and critique the trade-offs and limitations of the design**. Examples: a bicycle carrier, a small ventilation fan, a garden water pump, the heating nozzle of a 3D printer, or an elevator counterweight. This is not a task of actual fabrication or safety judgment.

Outline of the review report: ① **Function and specifications**: what the system does, and the required values such as load, temperature, flow rate, and speed. ② **Modeling assumptions**: what has been simplified (static loads, one degree of freedom, estimated friction coefficient). ③ **Calculations by field**: stress and safety factor, heat flow and temperature, flow rate and pressure loss, natural frequency and operating frequency. ④ **Interactions between fields**: how a choice in one field affects the others. ⑤ **Control and operation**: if needed, what is measured and what is adjusted. ⑥ **Risk and safety margin**: safety factor, worst-case conditions, and consequences of failure. ⑦ **Critique and improvement**: the conditions under which the assumptions break down, and what should be checked in the next step (experiments, more precise analysis).

Features of a good report: every number has units and a basis. Assumptions are not hidden, and the report states how much each assumption affects the conclusion. The **trade-offs** between fields are stated explicitly (for example, making a structure lighter increases vibration, and making a pipe thinner increases pump power). Where safety is involved, judgments are conservative, and the need for "further verification" is clearly written.
This task is not graded. The submitted text is saved only on this device, and you can view it again under "My progress" in "My notes."

checks.prompt: In three to five sentences, summarize the hypothetical mechanical system you will review: its functional specifications, its numerical values, and the three fields you will review.
checks.hint: As in the model structure, write in the order of specifications → fields → assumptions.
checks.explanation: Clear specifications and assumptions are needed before the calculations can be reviewed.
checks.model: We review a hypothetical garden water pump system. The specification is to raise 20 L per minute to a water tank 3 m high, with a pipe diameter of 0.02 m and a length of 15 m. The three fields to review are fluid (velocity, Reynolds number, friction loss, and pump power), structure (bending stress of the bracket that fixes the pump), and vibration (pump rotation speed and the natural frequency of the bracket). The friction factor is estimated from the turbulent value for a smooth pipe, and minor losses are assumed to be 20%.
